e.etymology: From Welsh gwen, the feminine of gwyn, meaning white, fair or blessed. It is also a short form of Gwendolen and Guinevere.
namesakes: Gwen Stefani (singer and No Doubt frontwoman)

assoc.t: Gwen Stefani, singer and No Doubt frontwoman

e.etymology: From Latin Paulina, the feminine of Paulinus, a derivative of Paulus, small. Borne by a third-century saint and common today in Spanish and Polish.
In Finnish, Aila comes from Sami, as a variant of Aili. In the US it is also used as a spelling of Ayla or as a sound-alike of Isla.
A modern spelling of Cason, an English surname altered from the Norfolk place name Cawston. It rose with the sound it shares with Mason, Jason and Grayson.
From the Irish surname O Seaghdha, descendant of Seaghdha, a byname usually explained as hawk-like or admirable.

assoc.t: shea butter, the skin-care ingredient
Shea Stadium, former home of the New York Mets

e.etymology: A late 20th-century coinage, shortened from Skyler or built on Sky with an -la ending. Skyler itself comes from the Dutch surname Schuyler, scholar.

assoc.t: Bayer's hormonal IUD
Pokemon gym leader

e.note: Skyla is also the brand name of a hormonal IUD sold in the US.

e.etymology: From the English word junior, Latin for younger, long a nickname for a son named after his father and then a given name in its own right.
namesakes: Junior Seau (Hall of Fame NFL linebacker)

assoc.t: Jr., the suffix for a son named after his father
a third-year student in high school or college

e.note: An everyday word and a generic nickname for any son, so it can read as a title more than a name.

e.etymology: From Latin Johanna, a variant of Joanna, from Greek Ioanna and Hebrew Yochanah, God is gracious. It is the feminine of Johannes, the source of John.
namesakes: Johanna Mason (victor in The Hunger Games)

e.etymology: The English word loyal used as a name, from Old French loial and Latin legalis, lawful. It had a run as a virtue name around 1900 and has returned since the 2010s.

assoc.t: the everyday English word loyal

e.etymology: A spelling of Amaya, the Spanish form of Basque Amaia, a place name and the heroine of an 1879 historical novel. Amaia means the end in Basque.
A spelling of Derek, borrowed in the Middle Ages from a Low German form of Theodoric, ruler of the people, and revived in the 19th century.

assoc.t: derrick, the tower over an oil well or a lifting crane

e.etymology: A form of Biblical Hazael, Hebrew for God has seen, a king of Aram in the Old Testament; the spelling Azael comes from the Greek Bible. In the US it is used mainly by Latino families.
e.note: Close in sound to Azazel and Azrael, a demon and the angel of death in religious lore.

e.etymology: From Arabic, the feminine of Samir, a companion in evening conversation, from samara, to talk at night. A separate Sanskrit word samira means breeze.
namesakes: Samira Wiley (actress in Orange Is the New Black and The Handmaid's Tale)

e.etymology: From the Slavic root mil, dear or kind; the feminine counterpart of Milan. Long used across the Slavic countries and also in Italy and Brazil.
A modern American coinage joining Bryn, from a Welsh word for hill, with the -leigh ending; a spelling of Brynlee.
A recent American name with no single source; it echoes Azariah and Amari. Azari is also the Persian word for Azerbaijani.
From Sanskrit veda, knowledge, the name of the oldest Hindu scriptures. In the US it was in use by the 1890s and has returned since the 2010s.

assoc.t: the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism

e.etymology: Made familiar by Nala, the lioness in Disney's The Lion King (1994). It is often said to mean gift in Swahili, which is not established; Nala is also a king in the Sanskrit epic Mahabharata.

assoc.t: lioness in Disney's The Lion King

e.note: Among the most popular names for pet dogs and cats in the US.

e.etymology: From Latin Caelia, the feminine of the Roman family name Caelius, probably from caelum, heaven. Shakespeare brought it into English with As You Like It.
namesakes: Celia (Rosalind's cousin in Shakespeare's As You Like It)

assoc.t: Celia Cruz, the Queen of Salsa

e.meaning: from Keaton, an English place name
e.etymology: From an English surname, a variant of Caton or Keeton or taken from Keaton in Devon, a place name possibly joining Welsh cae, enclosure, with Middle English toun, farmstead.

assoc.t: actors Michael Keaton and Diane Keaton (surname)

e.etymology: The Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Albert, shortened from Adalberto, from Frankish Athalaberht: athal, noble, and berht, bright.
From the Latin name Valentinus, from valens, strong or healthy. It is the form of Valentine used in French, German, Russian and Romanian, after the third-century Saint Valentine.
namesakes: Val Chmerkovskiy (Dancing with the Stars champion, born Valentin)

e.etymology: From the color word and the English surname Grey or Gray, first a nickname for a gray-haired man; the surname can also come from Graye in Normandy. Grey is the British spelling of the color.

assoc.t: the color gray, in its British spelling
Grey's Anatomy, the long-running TV medical drama
Christian Grey of Fifty Shades of Grey

e.etymology: A form of the Biblical Hebrew name Leah, usually explained as weary or wild cow; it is the usual spelling in French, German and Scandinavia. Lea is also an old English word for a meadow.
namesakes: Lea Thompson (Back to the Future actress)
Lea Salonga (Broadway star and singing voice of Disney's Jasmine and Mulan)

e.etymology: The English word love used as a name, as the Puritans did in the 1600s. In Sweden Love, said LOO-veh, is a separate boys' name related to Louis.

assoc.t: the everyday English word love

e.note: An everyday word and term of endearment, so expect puns; it also means zero in tennis.

e.etymology: The English number word used as a name, often chosen as a lucky or Biblically complete number; it rose after 2000. Seven is also a Turkish name meaning loving.

assoc.t: the number 7
Se7en, the 1995 serial-killer thriller film
Seinfeld episode where George wants to name a baby Seven
Seven of Nine in Star Trek: Voyager

e.note: A number as a name draws jokes; Seinfeld built an episode around George wanting to name his child Seven.

e.etymology: From French Adèle, the equivalent of Adela, from a Germanic root meaning noble; the same root is behind Adelaide and Alice.
namesakes: Adele (British singer of Hello and Rolling in the Deep)

assoc.t: British singer of Hello and Rolling in the Deep

e.etymology: A modern American combination of Ada, or the Adal- of names like Adaline and Adalyn, with the -lee ending.
From Bill with the -ie ending, a pet form of William, from Germanic wil, will, and helm, helmet. Once a nickname for boys and girls alike, it is now mostly a girls' name.

assoc.t: women's razor and body-care brand

e.etymology: A feminine form of Carl with -y, taken up in the later 20th century, and a pet form of Carla and Carlotta. Carl comes from a Germanic word for a free man. Carly Simon's fame helped it spread.
namesakes: Carly Simon (singer-songwriter of You're So Vain)
Carly Rae Jepsen (Call Me Maybe singer)
Carly Shay (title character of Nickelodeon's iCarly)

assoc.t: iCarly, the Nickelodeon sitcom

e.etymology: From Latin rex, king, coined as a given name in the 19th century.

assoc.t: T. rex, the dinosaur Tyrannosaurus rex
the green dinosaur in Toy Story
a stock name for a pet dog

e.note: Long a stock name for dogs, and children will connect it with T. rex.

e.etymology: A spelling of Lachlan, from Scottish Gaelic Lochlann, land of the lochs, the Gaels' name for Norway and the Vikings who came from it.
